newsitem.title: zaire: Zaire rebels claim new conquests, foreigners leave.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels claim new conquests, foreigners leave.

text.p: Zairean rebels said on Tuesday they had driven government troops out of two more towns in the northeast and panicked foreigners pulled out of the area for fear of killing, looting and mayhem.
Commander Jean Kabongo, special security adviser to rebel leader Laurent Kabila, told Reuters in the town of Goma that both Bunia and Walikale had fallen to rebel forces.
Missionary sources said there was shooting in Bunia on Monday, apparently by the Zairean army, but they could not confirm that rebels had taken either of the two towns.

Kabongo said on Monday that the rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces, had captured parts of the city of Kisangani, the biggest in the region, but aid agencies said on Tuesday the city remained in government hands.
The commander repeated his claim on Tuesday. "We are in and around Kisangani... There will be a big combat for Kisangani but our forces have been there, around it, for a month," he said.
"Our forces will be advancing around Kisangani... We have also got Bunia and Walikale," he added.

The northernmost town confirmed in rebel hands is Beni, 220 km (135 miles) north of Goma. Bunia is 140 km (90 miles) northeast of Beni and Walikale is 130 km (80 miles) northwest of Goma, on the road to Kisangani.

On Monday both Laurent and Kabongo said Walikale was giving the rebel forces trouble. Kabongo said they had bypassed it to reach Kisangani, site of a major air base and the government's most likely rallying point in any counter-offensive.
Aid agency sources said one aid organisation, Aviation sans Frontieres, was pulling out of Kisangani because of the danger.

The United Nations Children's Fund UNICEF in the Zairean capital Kinshasa said it pulled its last two personnel out of Kisangani on Monday to do some work in Kinshasa but the timing was related to the unrest.

"UNICEF is very concerned about the security situation in Kisangani," said Steven Allen, UNICEF representative in Kinshasa. "On Monday staff reported shooting between different elements of the Zairean army, apparently sparked by the arrival of wounded and dead Zairean soldiers from Beni," he added.

Another aviation charity, Mission Aviation Fellowship, said on Tuesday it had evacuated its planes and personnel from the town of Niakunde, 25 km (15 miles) west of Bunia, for fear of trouble as ill-disciplined Zairean troops retreat in disarray.
"We finished the evacuation late yesterday -- six planes and 12 families. The planes have gone to Entebbe (in Uganda)," an official of the charity told Reuters.
"The Zairean soldiers say they are afraid of the rebels and of the local population, in case they turn against them," added a missionary source with information from the Bunia area.

"Kisangani appears to be unstable. Some planes and some staff have been shot at. We're also hearing that the DSP (Division Speciale Presidentielle) has been sent up to Kisangani to disarm the government soldiers," he added.
The DSP is the special and well-equipped military unit assigned to protect President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is recovering from illness in the south of France.
Another piece of evidence from travellers also cast doubt on the credibility of the rebels' latest statements.
"It can't be true (that the rebels are in Kisangani). We sent a team to Kisangani yesterday and it was very normal at the airport," said one missionary source.
"They moved one tonne of medicines all the way from Kisangani to Lubutu and there was no sign of rebels," added the source. Lubutu is about halfway between Kisangani and Walikale.
"The rebels couldn't reach Kisangani without going through Lubutu," said the source.

The rebellion broke out in October among Zaireans of Rwandan origin whom the government was trying to repatriate, along with more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees who took refuge in Zaire after the genocide of Tutsis in 1994.
On the southern front, the rebels say they have captured the gold and diamond mining centre of Kamituga, carving out a swath of territory running more than 400 km (250 miles) north-south.
The fighting has dispersed hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans into the countryside. Canada is trying to lead a multinational force to find and help them.

But more than two weeks after the U.N. Security Council launched the multinational force, a mere 200 or so Canadians have arrived in the region but are still hundreds of miles from where food may be needed.
A spokesman for the Canadian-led force said 206 Canadians were in place at the force's headquarters at Entebbe airport on the shores of Lake Victoria in Uganda.
